FIRE RED, ASM EDITION

A Pokémon FireRed-like game written in x86-64 assembly. No libc, no engine, raw syscalls. Every picture is AI-generated Game Boy Advance style pixel art — and the creatures are drawn as pixels, not as text: each terminal cell carries two colours (foreground on top, background below), so a cell is two square pixels instead of one character.

How a picture becomes pixels

  1. A generated PNG lands in art_src/.
  2. tools/art2cells.py samples it at one square pixel per half-cell: the grid is width pixels across and height*2 down, so the pixels come out square — which is what makes it look like an image instead of characters.
  3. Each half-cell is quantised to the game's 16-colour palette, then the two halves of a cell are packed into one 32-bit word: idx | (fg<<16) | (bg<<24), where idx is 1 for a two-colour cell, 2 when both halves match, 0 for transparent.
  4. blit_art_hb turns that into screen state: it writes the U+2580 upper-half-block glyph and an attribute byte (bg<<4)|fg, so the top pixel takes the foreground colour and the bottom pixel the background colour.
  5. Text is unaffected — the dialogue, menus and the overworld tiles still use ordinary glyphs, and the two kinds of cell sit side by side in the same framebuffer.

make art regenerates the tables, make test runs the 19 headless playthroughs, make tour re-dumps the walkthrough. Every screenshot above is a real frame from the actual binary, rendered through the same ANSI palette the game emits.
